items.title: Carroll Dunham Calls His Filthy Formalism “Abstraction with a Hard-On”
items.summary:
I thought it best to confess up front that I was still forming an opinion about his work. Carroll Dunham took that like a gentleman. He is familiar, he made clear to me during ourranginginterview, with the two main camps of interpretation about his potty-mouthed paintings and drawings: 1) that he is a high formalist with an ear for the unconscious seldom rivaled since Surrealism, and 2) that he is a simple vulgarian.

“I’m lucky people even want to write about my work,” Dunham said. “I made the paintings. They can say whatever they want.” At 76, Dunham is thin, likable, and frank. He has a sharp, deadpan face framed by transition lenses and Beckettian white hair. When we spoke in his studio in Connecticut, he wore a silk suit in the shade of gray-green the French call caca d’oie , the shirt buttoned only in the top half, cholo style, with chunky sneakers in the same shade.

The spacious upstairs had been given over to small abstract sculptures he was making out of aluminum sheeting with assistants. It was July, and Dunham was between two capstone surveys of a long career. A show of his drawings spanning 1974 to 2024 had recently come down at the Art Institute of Chicago, while curators at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, were finalizing a survey of his paintings from 1983 to the present for December. It was the kind of summary moment an artist is lucky to be alive for.

Carroll Dunham in his home studio in Cornwall, Connecticut. 

Photo Laurie Simmons 

Since the ’90s, Dunham’s best-known pictures have starred carefully framed cartoon penises, vaginas, and anuses…
items.t: Carroll Dunham Calls His Filthy Formalism “Abstraction with a Hard-On”

items.title: Batima Zaurbekova’s Textiles Meld Traditional Kazakh Techniques with Modernist Influences, Defying Easy Categorization
items.summary:
How does an artist sustain five decades of artistic production while remaining faithful to her cultural heritage? For Batima Zaurbekova, one of Kazakhstan’s most respected artists, the answer seems to be an unrelenting commitment to her craft. “You can’t be lazy,” the 80-year-old artist told me during a recent conversation.

That maxim is borne out in “Threads of Heritage,” a retrospective of more than 80 works at the Abylkhan Kasteyev National Museum of Arts in Almaty, Kazakhstan. Her largest exhibition to date, it features the textiles she is known for as well as drawings and paintings. Curated by Alina Fedorovich, a curator at the Museum of Moscow, the exhibition traces a career in which tapestry becomes both a repository of cultural memory and a vehicle for artistic reinvention.

Rooted in traditional Kazakh textiles, her practice is also shaped by the influences of modernist painting and music, moving fluidly between abstraction and figuration and in turn, defying easy categorization. Her tapestries hold seemingly disparate influences, transforming traditional motifs into a distinct visual language. Ornamental Rug (1969), for example, revives motifs associated with horses, spiritual symbolism, and petroglyphs depicting mountain goats. Completed just after her graduation and the earliest work in the exhibition, Ornamental Rug provides a recognizable reference to the country’s landscape via the distinctive horns of the wild argali , a local mountain goat, while distilling these forms into rhythmic, stylized arrangements. The work’s title foregrounds the relationship…

items.title: Banish gloom with Paul Foot’s teetering towers of nonsense in fizzy show The Future
items.summary:
Soho theatre, London
The standup throws himself into ‘13 or 14 pieces of humour’ that confirm his gifts for escalating everyday apercus into absurd delights

Paul Foot made quite the impression with 2023’s Dissolve, a mid-career breakout from his oddball groove. The Future confirms the 52-year-old as a comic any audience could enjoy, and – to some degree – develops his newfound interest in the real world and the circumstances of his own life. Not that it begins with any seriousness of purpose, as our host throws himself into a series of escalating set pieces built on everyday apercus – how reassuring we find it, say, when a Chinese restaurant is frequented by Chinese diners. Then comes the swerve, which is less well integrated, and less remarkable, than in the show’s predecessor, but affecting nonetheless.

Before that, the first half is all about Foot’s free-standing bits (“about 13 or 14 pieces of humour”, he calls them): concentrated bursts of observational comedy, in which he inflates a workaday premise to absurdity and beyond. The etiquette of British funerals; over-excitement at food served on sizzling hot-plates – Foot constructing teetering towers of nonsense from it all with a voice and range of facial expression evoking British comedy at its ooh-missus, nudge-nudge heyday.

items.title: Rare Marie Antoinette ‘Breast Bowl’ Hammers for $2.47 M. in Paris, Surpassing Top Estimate
items.summary:
One of the last known “Breast Bowls” still in private hands that once belonged to Queen Marie Antoinette has just hammered for €2.25 million ($2.47 million), or €2,945 million with fees ($3.23 million), at the Coutau-Begarie & Associés evening auction in Paris’s Hôtel Drouot, beating its high estimate of €2 million ($2.19 million).

Legend has it that this series of 18th-century porcelain bowls, made by the Royal Sèvres manufacturers, was modeled after the ill-fated French queen’s real breasts. While no documented proof of such a legend exists, the so-called “ jatte-téton ” or “nipple bowls,” painted in fleshy light pink with an areola and nipple at the tip, do have a surrealistic, convincingly realistic quality, despite a too-perfectly circular shape.

Made in 1787, the bowl in question was in fact inspired by ancient Greek mastos , or breast-shaped drinking cups used at banquets dating back to the 6th century BC. It is one of four highly prized jatte-tétons delivered that year and in 1788, destined for the royal “pleasure dairy” in Rambouillet, near Versailles, that King Louis XVI gifted to Marie Antoinette. There, per the fashion of the time, nobility would gather to socialize and taste an assortment of fine milk, cream, and cheese delicacies prepared for them.

The rare breast bowl comes from the collection of French dealer Claude Meyer, who passed away in November 2025. His children happened upon it while going through boxes of storage, and learned that their late father, whose Paris gallery closed in the 1990s, had never offered it for sale. It is unclear how Meyer…

items.title: Mammy Goose is well and truly cooked in Glasgow’s incredibly random Aladdin
items.summary:
King’s theatre, Glasgow
The offensive stereotypes have been ditched but this glitzy panto starring Elaine C Smith shoehorns in plenty of irrelevant material

Staging a traditional Aladdin in 2026 is problematic. All those laundry scenes, acrobatics and faux Chinese names have the unpleasant whiff of orientalism. In that sense, it is good to see this glitzy mainstream panto, scripted by Alan McHugh and Harry Michaels for Crossroads, ditching all that. If only it had not thrown the genie out with the bath water.

Stereotypes aside, Aladdin can still be a gripping coming-of-age story about greed and gullibility, poverty and power. The stakes can be loaded with deceit, jeopardy and cunning. In this version, set in the land of Pantomania, almost none of that survives.

items.title: Lisa Marei Schmidt Appointed Director of Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee
items.summary:
Lisa Marei Schmidt, the director of the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, is leaving her post to take over as director of the Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern, Switzerland, starting August 1, 2027. She will also chair the management board of both institutions and be responsible for their artistic direction. The Renzo Piano-designed Zentrum Paul Klee holds the world’s largest collection of works by Klee, while the Kunstmuseum Bern is Switzerland’s oldest fine art museum.

Schmidt has been at the Brücke-Museum since 2017 and has orchestrated many exhibitions, including Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019), Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22), and Confiscated and Forgotten: The Female Artists Targeted by the Nazi ‘Degenerate Art’ Campaign , which opens April 30 to July 25, 2027. The Berlin museum is currently exhibiting Swedish Modernism until February 28, 2027, with a focus on the artist groups De unga (The Young Ones), De åtta (The Eight) and the Gothenburg Colorists. “To me, museums are places where art and people meet. They provide space for encounters, new perspectives and dialogue across society,” said Schmidt, in a statement on Thursday. “I very much look forward to getting to know the two remarkable institutions, the teams and the people in the City and Canton of Bern. Together, I hope to build on the Kunstmuseum Bern’s and Zentrum Paul Klee’s distinctive qualities and shape their future development.”

Schmidt was chosen out of 97 candidates who applied for the position. Jonathan Gimmel, president of the…
items.t: Lisa Marei Schmidt Appointed Director of Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee

items.title: At the Broad, Six Decades of Art Question the Myth of Progress
items.summary:
Two weeks after the 1992 Los Angeles uprising, Los Angeles Times reporter Janny Scott published an essay confronting her own complacency toward the city’s stark inequalities. For years, she’d witnessed the chasm widen between women carrying $3,500 handbags and those wearing trash bags; from her “nice neighborhood where the helicopters don’t come,” she did little to address the disparity. Still, the unrest that followed the acquittal of four LAPD officers charged with beating Rodney King seemed to have broken through the collective apathy. Angelenos, she wrote, were suddenly talking about “things that matter”: race, guilt, poverty, urban policy, to name a few. Despite history offering little reason for optimism, Scott confessed to a sense of hope: “I’m nurturing my first illusion.”

More than three decades later, artist Guadalupe Rosales found a copy of the newspaper containing Scott’s article on eBay. The headlines “Seeing Ourselves” and “Has the Myth Been Shattered?” registered the same discrepancy she sensed between what she remembered as a child growing up in East LA and how the press perpetuated myths about the city’s seeming collectivity. Rosales was 11 years old in 1992, and she has a distinct memory of her mother rushing the family home from school as smoke stained the usually sun-drenched California sky. As an adult, Rosales has amassed an archive of clippings, photographs, and other ephemera of Chicanx youth culture—much of it crowdsourced through social media—that serves as both a bulwark against that dissonance and a counter to historical erasure and amnesia.…
items.t: At the Broad, Six Decades of Art Question the Myth of Progress

items.title: Kevin Love’s Miami Home Features Work by Antony Gormley, Rashid Johnson, Ed Ruscha and Richard Prince
items.summary:
Ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, which runs from December 4 to 6, NBA star Kevin Love reflects on his journey into art collecting, which has made him the proud owner of works by Antony Gormley, Rashid Johnson, Ed Ruscha and George Condo.

In an interview with Art Basel’s Miami Beach Magazine , the five-time NBA All-Star and 2016 NBA champion and his wife, Kate Bock, opened their Miami home to reporters, displaying an impressive art collection of paintings and sculptures. He reveals that he has Ed Ruscha’s The End (2021) hanging over his bed, a painting to which he feels a personal connection. “I hate to be one of those people who watches a lot of TV in bed, but we do, and The End has a connection to Ruscha and to film. It’s also very literal: It’s the end of the day, you’re in bed,” Love said. “And it’s a reminder: I’m thinking about the end of a career. Whether it’s in two months or two years, it’s there; and with that, new beginnings as well. I’ve always loved his work. He’s a great man, he’s empathetic and supportive. My wedding gift to my wife, Kate, was a Ruscha.” Love is also the owner of three other Ruscha artworks: Woman on Fire (2024), He Enjoys the Co. of Women (2025) and The Girl Always Did Have Good Taste (2021).

Kevin Love poses in front of Hank Willis Thomas, O! thus be it ever , 2021. 

Courtesy Nick Mele for the Art Basel Miami Beach Magazine

items.title: Hoor Al Qasimi Named Curator of 2028 Venice Biennale
items.summary:
Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale, the world’s biggest recurring art exhibition running from April 8 to November 26, 2028. Al Qasimi is also president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation , a member of the United Arab Emirates’s Sharjawi royal family and president of the Sharjah Museums Authority.

The board of La Biennale di Venezia said it met on November 20 to pick Al Qasimi on the recommendation of president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco. Al Qasimi will be tasked with curating the 62nd edition of the exhibition and will take on the title of director of the visual arts department.

“La Biennale di Venezia is a place where the world converges with art through its diverse visions. Throughout her career, Hoor Al Qasimi has succeeded in creating a caravanserai of geographies and the Universal, giving voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected,” said Buttafuoco in a statement on Thursday. “Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people. I also recognize in her a quality of balance and composure, namely the vibrant presence of mīzān (inner harmony), which finds its strength in relationships.”

The taking of an art biennale is nothing new to Al Qasimi. In 2024, she was appointed by the Biennale of Sydney as the artistic director of the exhibition’s 25th edition, which ran from March 7 to June 8, 2026. However, the Venice Biennale is…

items.title: The greatest stage invasion! How theatres are bringing audiences into the action, from Jesus Christ Superstar to Cloud 9
items.summary:
A wave of shows, including High School Musical and Rent, are upping the drama by placing viewers alongside actors. What are the risks and rewards?

In the socially distanced summer of 2020, Jesus Christ Superstar was staged at Regent’s Park in London for a hugely pruned audience. Like the actors, we were kept two metres apart. It was a triumphant but extremely strange experience – not least from my current perspective. I’m standing on stage at Theatre Royal Drury Lane, jostling alongside other theatregoers, watching a miraculous revival of the same production. But this time, 75 audience members have been given a spot within the scaffold-style set for the show, beneath the musicians and almost side by side with the cast. We feel the energy of the ensemble’s dance moves, seem to join the crowd of Jesus’s followers – and those who conspire against him – and come extraordinarily close to the musical’s star, Sam Ryder, who rests right by my feet after his solo Gethsemane. It’s as close as I’ve been to the beating heart of a big West End production.

Until, that is, the following week when I watch the captivating revival of Rent at the Tom Stoppard theatre from one of 82 audience seats arranged in a semicircle on stage. (Mine is just beneath a shelf bearing candle-filled wine bottles – a…

items.title: Smithsonian Head Assures Staff of Independence After Glimpse of White House Overhaul Plan
items.summary:
Outgoing Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III reasserted the institution’s independence in a letter to his staff after a leaked document from a Trump aide laid out a sweeping overhaul of its programming and personnel.

“The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in the letter, which the New York Times reviewed and first reported. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”

The document, titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan,” was photographed on a laptop that a Trump aide was using on the Washington Metro. As first reported by ProPublica , its 25-item action list includes plans to dismiss top curators and administrators, among them Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, whom the White House has accused of promoting “radical activist ideology.” 

The plan also calls for a new permanent exhibit, “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance,” and another on “Great Families of American History.” It envisions a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington at the museum’s entrance, which would fulfill a request Trump made in September.

The plan appears to be a work in progress: Photos show the aide brainstorming additions in a notebook. One handwritten entry seems to read “No X-rated exhibition policy,” an apparent callback to a particularly contentious stretch of Hartig’s testimony, when lawmakers questioned her about images of…
items.t: Smithsonian Head Assures Staff of Independence After Glimpse of White House Overhaul Plan

items.title: Tate Liverpool Plans Fall 2027 Reopening With Surrealism Survey
items.summary:
Tate Liverpool will reopen in fall 2027 after a £30 million transformation with the exhibition “Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds,” a nod to the museum’s inaugural Surrealist show in 1988.

The surrealism exhibition will run from fall 2027 to spring 2028 and include works by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray. According to Tate Liverpool, the show will also explore the “important role of surrealism in the history of theater and dance” through the movement’s major commissions for stage sets and costumes. Also on view will be Dorothea Tanning’s costume designs for the ballet The Witch , photographs of Sheila Legge performing as the “Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal” at the opening of the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London, and material from the archive of Ted Joans.

“Surrealism invites us to see the world differently and what better way to reopen Tate Liverpool. This exhibition will spark imaginations, surprise visitors and reward curiosity, offering a fresh perspective on one of art’s most celebrated movements. It also brings a wonderful echo of the surrealist exhibition that opened our gallery in 1988, while taking visitors on an exciting new journey,” said Jemima Pyne, interim director of the Tate Liverpool, in a statement.

Tate Liverpool closed in October 2023 and was scheduled to reopen in 2025, but fundraising difficulties pushed the date back to 2027. The architecture firm 6a architects is redesigning the gallery’s home, an 1846 warehouse on the Royal Albert Dock, as part of a £35 million ($46.5 million) renovation.
items.t: Tate Liverpool Plans Fall 2027 Reopening With Surrealism Survey

items.title: Helen Fraser obituary
items.summary:
Actor whose career ranged from the film of Billy Liar to the Royal Shakespeare Company and TV roles in Bad Girls and Coronation Street

The actor Helen Fraser, who has died aged 84 after suffering from Alzheimer’s disease, made her first impression on screen in the 1963 kitchen sink movie Billy Liar, as one of two fiancees dumped by Billy (Tom Courtenay), the daydreaming title character, in favour of his free-spirited former girlfriend (Julie Christie). She went on to enjoy a long career as a character actor on television, best remembered as the miserable prison warder Sylvia Hollamby, nicknamed “Bodybag”, in Bad Girls (1999-2006).

Billy Liar was based on Keith Waterhouse’s novel about an undertaker’s assistant who escapes into a world of fantasy to relieve the tedium of his life in a north of England town. With Willis Hall, Waterhouse had already turned it into a stage play by the time Fraser was cast in the film version as the sheltered Barbara, while Gwendolyn Watts played the more outspoken Rita.

items.title: Shahzia Sikander Sculpture in St. Louis Generates Protests and Counterprotests
items.summary:
Activists against women’s right to choose in relation to their reproductive rights protested a sculpture by Shahzia Sikander in St. Louis this week, calling for the removal of the 18-foot-tall work titled Witness (2023).

As reported by St. Louis’s First Alert 4 , protesters associating the sculpture with pro-choice abortion rights gathered outside the home base of Rung for Women, a nonprofit devoted to women’s career development that hosts it. As the organization describes itself on its website, “Too many women are unfulfilled, unhappy, and underpaid in their jobs, but afraid to take the leap into the unknown. We designed a program to guide motivated women through a process to start working in exciting careers and get paid what they’re worth.”

First Alert 4 quoted an activist with a group called Students for Life America associating Sikander’s sculpture with the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. “Her skirt spells Hava, which is Eve, the first female rebel, to breathe life,” said Reagan Barklage, who related the work to the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. “It’s just, you do not need to kill your children in order to breathe life. That’s actually the exact opposite of what that means.”

She continued: “We’re alarmed that this is what they’re choosing to use to represent our city. We do not stand for these pro-abortion rights. And we’re trying to stand for women and true empowerment.”

A counterprotester thought otherwise. “We’re here because this organization that’s located on this block has every right to display whatever artwork they want on their…

items.title: Bill Bailey is an absolute master of musical mischief – this crowd hangs on every twang
items.summary:
SEC Armadillo, Glasgow
The comedian’s new concoction, Vaudevillean, mixes offbeat historical diversions, topical gags and virtuoso musical flights with warmth and absurdity

Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist.

The 61-year-old’s current show is called Vaudevillean, and gestures are made towards justifying that title, with reference to the French poet Olivier Basselin and the 1453 battle of Castillon. (You don’t get this with Michael McIntyre.) Like vaudeville, the show certainly has variety to recommend it. But really, this offering differs little from many a previous Bailey outing, and finds our host again following his nose from one unlikely musical experiment to another, via nuggets of topical standup and anecdotes from his storied life.

Touring Europe until 2 May
items.t: Bill Bailey is an absolute master of musical mischief – this crowd hangs on every twang

items.title: Sir Stanley Wells obituary
items.summary:
Eminent Shakespeare scholar and author who brought together the worlds of academia and the theatre

In 1978 Oxford University Press made Stanley Wells, who has died aged 96, director of a Shakespeare department specially created so that he could produce a new edition of the complete works.

Starting from scratch, he went back to the early printed copies, the quartos and folios, and thought through every editorial and textual decision – how to modernise the spelling and punctuation, and edit stage directions and speakers’ names, while giving the rationales for emendations. The single volume Complete Shakespeare appeared in 1986, edited by Stanley, with Gary Taylor, John Jowett and William Montgomery. It proved to be groundbreaking, startling and controversial.

items.summary:
Royal Court theatre, London
Ryan Calais Cameron’s ‘true(ish)’ account of a charismatic freedom fighter’s plan to take a Zambian crew to the moon never quite lifts off

Ryan Calais Cameron has proved himself a playwright of stratospheric talent. His previous plays For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy and Retrograde both streaked their way into the West End. This new one is filled with mighty ambition but does not lift off in the same way.

It is based on what he calls a “true(ish)” story. The figure of Edward Mukuka Nkoloso (Lucian Msamati) is taken from Zambian history. A freedom fighter for the nation’s independence in the 1960s, he set up a national academy for science and trained a group of “afronauts” in the hope of beating the US and the Soviet Union in the race to reach the moon. Nkoloso, a kind of Dead Poets Society inspiration figure here, picks 17-year-old Martha (Ama Qamata) for the mission.

items.title: Simon Brodkin: ‘Which of my pranks went badly wrong? Well, Boris Johnson became PM after the Theresa May one’
items.summary:
The character comedian AKA Lee Nelson handed May a P45 and threw golf balls at Donald Trump. He explains why the pranking’s now on ice – and which funny footballers inspired him

How did you get into comedy?
I was booted out of every class for making jokes and then I discovered, at medical school, there is such a thing as a career in comedy. I was encouraged by being able to entertain the patients and went straight from that into comedy.

Who did you admire when you were starting out?
It was always the character comedians: Sacha Baron Cohen, Ricky Gervais, Steve Coogan. On the circuit Al Murray was doing the Pub Landlord. I admired anyone doing characters who could be dropped into multiple situations. As I started doing character comedy myself, I was inspired by people who might not have known how funny they were, such as a big batch of Premier League footballers from Beckham to Gerrard to Rooney.

Simon Brodkin: Unleashed is at the Apollo, London, on 13 December and 11 March and on tour in the UK until 26 May

items.title: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
items.summary:
Royal & Derngate, Northampton
The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties

Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake.

That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten.
items.t: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
